title: Why "I Don't Know Why The AI Did That" Is Now A Legal Risk
description:
Telling a regulator, a lawyer, or a customer that you do not know why your AI made a decision used to be an awkward answer. In 2026 it is a legal liability with real financial consequences.

Every agent action that affects a customer, spends money, or communicates externally needs to log three things. What the agent saw as input. The reasoning behind the decision it made. The output it produced. Without all three you cannot defend the decision in court, explain it to a regulator, or diagnose what went wrong when something breaks.

The tools that capture this are called agent traces. Langfuse, Galileo, Braintrust, and Phoenix all handle this. Pick one and wire it up before your agent goes live.

Treat agent traces the same way you treat financial records. You would not run a business without bookkeeping. Do not run an agent without traces.

top_comments.author: @g33xzi11a
top_comments.text: How about we just, I don’t know, not needlessly rush headlong into deploying pathologically dishonest and stupid technology into critical infrastructure. It’s just so brazenly hubristic and if any employee acted like these agents then they wouldn’t just be fired they’d probably be getting sued by their employers for breach of duty and possibly even prosecuted by the federal government for certain kinds of crimes like negligence. One of these things got 173 elementary school girls triple tapped by cruise missiles.
